newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets PM, Moscow mayor, busy agenda ahead.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets PM, Moscow mayor, busy agenda ahead.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin briefed Boris Yeltsin on Russia's pressing economic and political problems on Tuesday, the president's second day back in the Kremlin after his convalescence from heart surgery.

Keen to show he is firmly back at the helm, Yeltsin also held talks with Moscow mayor, Yuri Luzhkov, a key political ally, and plans to keep up a busy schedule in the coming days, his press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference.
"The president and prime minister discussed budgetary, financial and socio-economic problems facing the country during their one hour 40 minute meeting," Yastrzhembsky said.
The two men focused on wage and pension arrears and conditions in the cash-starved armed forces, he added.

Russia's elderly citizens are owed up to 14 trillion roubles ($2.5 billion) in unpaid pensions. Millions of state and private-sector workers have also been waiting many months to be paid. The government blames tax dodgers for the delays.
Yeltsin recently said managers of firms that did not pay their taxes were unfit for the job and should be sacked.
On Thursday he will chair a session of a special commission set up to improve tax collection and boost flagging state revenues.

Yeltsin's schedule this week also includes talks with Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, on Wednesday and a meeting with visiting Chinese premier Li Peng on Friday. Russia celebrates Christmas according to the Russian Orthodox calendar in early January.

The 65-year-old Yeltsin, dogged by ill health, has spent little time in the Kremlin since being re-elected for a second term in July. He had a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5 but said on Monday he was again "ready for battle".

Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin also discussed international issues on Tuesday, including NATO's planned eastward expansion -- which Moscow fiercely opposes -- and a scheduled March summit between the Russian leader and U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin planned to spend the New Year and Christmas holidays with his family and "without guests", probably at his Gorky 9 country residence near Moscow. Eastern Orthodox Russians celebrate Christmas on January 6 and 7.
"When the Kremlin tower clock chimes in the New Year the Yeltsin family traditionally goes outside to the Christmas tree. They will do this year what they always do," he said.
Yastrzhembsky added that Yeltsin had been deluged with invitations since his return to work but said it was impossible to accept them all for fear of "overloading" the president.

On a positive note for his government, still battling an economic slump five years after the collapse of the old Soviet Union, the lower house of parliament, the State Duma, is expected later this week to approve the 1997 draft budget.
After its third and final reading in the Duma -- dominated by Yeltsin's communist and nationalist foes -- the draft will pass to the more compliant upper house Federation Council.

Yeltsin and his government hope that 1997 will mark a turning point for the economy and that ordinary Russians, buffeted by years of turmoil, will start to feel the benefits of the country's painful shift towards the free market.
